newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Lack of monetary tools caused Israeli tender halt.
newsitem.headline: Lack of monetary tools caused Israeli tender halt.

text.p: The Bank of Israel's decision on Monday to temporarily halt its daily monetary tenders is a result of its limited ability to soak up excess liquidity through other means, central bank officials said.

Generally the central bank absorbs excess liquidity in the economy by issuing short-term Makam bills, which though they are like Treasury bills from the investors' point of view, do not finance government spending.

By law the Bank of Israel can issue up to 17.5 billion shekels worth of Makam bills. By mid-August the central bank had already issued bills for the value of about 16 billion shekels and is close to finishing its allocation.
An official at the central bank said that should the Treasury allow the central bank to issue more Makam bills the bank could renew the daily tenders.

"Instead of Makam bills we would be delighted to have open market operations, to influence the whole yield curve with open market operations as do other central banks. But we don't have this vehicle," said Gideon Schurr, central bank director of international affairs and external relations.

"In absence of this at least we need more Makam bills. But the Treasury is not willing to change the law which would allow us to issue more Makam bills. We don't have enough tools to face the increasing problem of a growing government deficit", he said.

The press has widely reported that the Treasury has resisted allowing the central bank to issue new Makam bills, fearing the high-yielding bills will compete with its own bonds and hinder government efforts to raise capital.
Last month the central bank cancelled seven monetary tenders because of surplus liquidity and in July it cancelled its weekly tenders to commercial banks.
In a statement the central bank said it would issue a notice when the daily tenders resume.

The excess liquidity is a result of high government expenditure, the statement said. The government's deficit in August soared to 2.089 billion shekels against a deficit of 879 million in July. In the first eight months of the year the government deficit reached 8.6 billion shekels, already above the deficit target of 7.6 billion shekels for the entire year.
The central bank has been pressuring the government to cut its budget deficit for 1996, saying it cannot lower interest rates in the current situation.
Last month the Treasury allowed the central bank to increase its offering of Makam bills, but only for the purpose of a special "security net" for the bond market.
The central bank has been repurchasing government bonds to stop bond prices from falling. The extra allocation of Makam bills is to soak up the liquidity from these repurchases.
